newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal budget gap shrinking, may not be enough.
newsitem.headline: Portugal budget gap shrinking, may not be enough.

text.p: Portugal has been more successful than most of Europe's southern flank in tackling its budget problems, but its chances of meeting the 1997 EMU entry test still look slim, most economists say.

Nobody doubts that when Finance Minister Antonio Sousa Franco presents his budget plan to parliament next month, the figures will show him hitting the deficit target of three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) next year.
But economist say that getting there will involve making assumptions about economic growth that are likely to prove too optimistic.

"I don't think it will be possible to achieve because they will be assuming an economic growth rate over which they have little control," said Banco Portugues de Investimento chief economist Rui Martins dos Santos.
The Socialist government, which is doggedly sticking to a growth forecast for around 2.75 percent this year, has said that it expects activity to pick up slightly in 1997 to three percent.
This is likely to be the figure for drawing up the budget blueprint which must be presented to parliament by October 15.

But with Europe's major economies still struggling to pick up momentum, most analysts see Portugal's economy growing this year at around 2.25 percent. Forecasts for next year average around 2.5 percent.

"It is very difficult to see a growth figure of 2.7-3.0 percent for next year," Dos Santos said. "Portugal would need to grow above three percent to cut the deficit significantly and I don't see them doing that," he added.

Much depends on how the deficit behaves in 1996, with the government hoping it can bring the gap between spending and income down to four percent to give it a good launching pad for its attempt to reach the Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) goal.
"If Portugal ends the year with (a deficit) around four percent, it will be in good shape," said economist Sally Wilkinson of UBS.
But Wilkinson, who described herself as generally "optimistic" on Portugal, still saw the country just missing out on the deficit target.
"The budget (programme) will be based on optimistic tax revenue forecasts," she said.
Nevertheless, the economist saw the government making an attempt at cutting back expenditure even if it was likely to go for the easy option of under-spending on capital investment.
The extra one percent of GDP that the government needs to find in 1997, either through increased revenues or lower spending, amounts to around 150 billion escudos ($985.5 million), or $one billion.

One Lisbon economist, who declined to be identified, said that the deficit goal could and should be attained but that this would involve a very tough line on public sector wages and some increase in taxation.
The Socialist government, which is just short of an outight parliamentary majority, has however repeatedly said that it does not want to raise taxes.

The main opposition party, the conservative Social Democrats, whose attitude could be vital to the budget's chances of passing through parliament, has said it is not prepared to back a financial plan that includes tax rises.

The government would also face tough opposition from unions if it sought to hold wage rises in the public sector to below inflation next year, a move that the Lisbon economist saw as necessary to reduce state spending. ($1=152.2 Escudo)
